title: From shared understanding to shared context · hancrafted
description: How work can speed up without guaranteeing a better result, how static and dynamic context differ, how to spot context that goes bad, and how an AI interview can help build a useful handover to take into a fresh chat.

DORA describes time moving from creating to checking ( ) ; the report does not establish that unclear specifications caused review load ( ) . The 28-document queue is illustrative.

Why precise and accurate requirements mattered before AI Every product translates an intent. How well that translation is written down decides the result. Both Precise Accurate Neither

Why precise and accurate requirements mattered before AI (1/3) Page 1 of 3 Value was always translation A product, a service or a lecture: each translates what a person wanted into something that solves the actual problem. 01 · What a person wanted The customer “I want to get to work without arriving sweaty.” One intent. 02 · What it was translated into Product E-bike Service Bike lease with a shower at the office Lecture Cycling to work in a suit Three translations.

Why precise and accurate requirements mattered before AI (2/3) Page 2 of 3 Defining and building Every effort splits into defining what to make and building it. AI speeds up building. For defining it can only guess what is in your head, unless it asks. 01 Defining Deciding what to make. AI can assist by asking. How far is your commute? Hills, or flat? 12 km, one big hill. “…as long as AI can’t read our minds.” 02 Building Making it. AI speeds it up a great deal. Frame Assemble Test ride More documents per hour at every station. Defining is Sales and Design, building is Build to Delivery. Clients can’t state it up front: they find out what they want by trying versions 48% of 228 companies name incomplete or hidden requirements as their top problem

Why precise and accurate requirements mattered before AI (3/3) Page 3 of 3 Precision and accuracy For this episode: precise means few open questions; accurate means aligned with the intended outcome. These are working definitions, not universal ones. Tight Loose Precise, off target Work order Road racer · frame M · carbon · no mudguards At the bench: The wrong bike, built perfectly. Precise and accurate Work order Commuter e-bike · frame M · 500 Wh · mudguards · rack At the bench: The right bike, no questions. Neither Work order A nice bike, quickly. At the bench: Wrong, and full of questions. Accurate, scattered Work order Something for the commute, with a motor? At the bench: Right in the end, after a dozen questions. Off the intent On the intent Up: precision , how few questions the sheet leaves open here Right: accuracy , whether it matches the rider's intent here A requirement that is wrong or missing does not stop the line, it ships the wrong bike ( ) . How much that costs depends on the job ( ) .
Context and requirements A useful but incomplete analogy: both ask what information supports the work, but an agent's context is not a requirements document. Context window Static Dynamic

Context and requirements (2/6) Page 2 of 6 Context engineering and requirements: a useful analogy Google’s definition: context engineering is “the practice of providing AI agents with rich, structured information about your codebase, architecture, conventions, and intent.” The comparison helps, but the two are not the same. Read as a requirement Codebase → the materials you already have Architecture → how the parts fit together Conventions → the house rules Intent → the goal Customer wants a city bike to ride to work, by Friday Same four outcomes as the dartboard Precise and accurate Context window “City bike, 54 cm frame, 7-speed hub, black, ready Friday.” Nothing to ask, nothing to guess. Precise, not accurate Context window “Road bike, 58 cm carbon frame, 22 speeds, ready Friday.” Clear, but the customer wanted a city bike. Accurate, not precise Context window “A comfortable bike for getting to work.” Right idea, ten questions left. Neither Context window “Something sporty, you know what I mean.” Vague and off target. Anthropic: aim for “the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens” that maximize the chance of the outcome you want ( ) . Researchers have proposed this analogy ( ) ; unlike a requirements document, the context window is a limited budget that can change while the agent works ( ) .

Context and requirements (3/6) Page 3 of 6 Static and dynamic context Static is set up before the shift; dynamic context can be fetched during it. You can limit sources and review what arrives: both land on the same bench. 07:00 · Before the shift Static The pinned instruction sheet Memory files The standing rules System prompt The first work order Initial prompt 10:30 · During the shift Dynamic Parts fetched from the storeroom Retrieval A call to a supplier Web search The folder of the current job Project folder

Context and requirements (4/6) Page 4 of 6 You run the bench You set up the bench and can limit what the AI may fetch. It can work without you watching every step; you can review the result. You AI worker On the bench: the work order, sheet version 3, four wrenches Held back: sheet version 1, the catalog of every model Your job What lands on the bench Brief it like a new colleague on day one. Where the work is heading Review the result; steer it if needed. Not your job You do not need to supervise every step. You can review the result. One GPT-4o test: more requirements, lower compliance One requirement: 98.7% compliance 19 requirements at once: 85.0% This is one test, not a prediction for every model or task. One study also found no general benefit from repository files that repeated discoverable information.

Context and requirements (5/6) Page 5 of 6 Context rot at the bench More context is not always more useful: four kinds of mess can arrive before or during the work. Names after Drew Breunig and IBM A wrong fact stuck in poisoning Too much that does not belong distraction Too many similar tools confusion Two instructions that disagree clash Static set up before the shift A wrong fact stuck in · poisoning A wrong screw size on the instruction sheet Too much that does not belong · distraction A binder of every bike model, when you build one Too many similar tools · confusion Fifty near-identical wrenches Two instructions that disagree · clash Old and new sheets both pinned up Dynamic arrives during the shift A wrong fact stuck in · poisoning A mislabeled box of screws Too much that does not belong · distraction Colleagues dropping by with questions Too many similar tools · confusion Ten crates of similar parts Two instructions that disagree · clash A shout of “rush it” against the sheet’s “check every piece”

Context and requirements (6/6) Page 6 of 6 Keeping the bench clean One cleanup per mess, and sometimes the cleanest fix is a clean bench. An illustrative one-to-one pairing from IBM Technology's video Other fixes exist too A wrong fact stuck in Validate Check the sheet against a real bike Too much that does not belong Compact Replace the binder with a one-page summary Too many similar tools Curate Keep only the wrenches the job needs Two instructions that disagree Prune Pull the old sheets down The cleanest fix Start at a clean bench: open a fresh chat and bring only the result, not the whole history. Long chat, leftovers and all Old chat 128K of 200K · 64% Fresh chat with the result Fresh chat 38K of 200K · 19%

Creating context for agents (1/3) Page 1 of 3 Meta prompting A separate session writes the context for you: the AI asks, you answer, and the bench gets one clean work order. Planning office · separate chat What must be ready before the spring rush? Every rental bike serviced and 40 repair slots bookable. Who books the slots, and how? The front desk, by phone and walk-in. What service checks and exact deadline should I include? Not decided yet—leave both open. You answer questions and review the draft. No prompt to write from scratch. Focused questions can help you say what you mean Stays in the office: questions, half-ideas, drafts Fresh chat only the work order crosses The line · bike bench Work order · Spring service week Goal Rental fleet serviced; 40 repair slots bookable Who Front desk books; service staffing not specified Must Service checks: to confirm Done when Exact deadline: to confirm Drafted from your answers; open details remain unconfirmed The AI worker can start from one page, not the whole conversation. You can review the result.

Creating context for agents (2/3) Page 2 of 3 Grill-me Matt Pocock’s grill-me skill: the AI asks questions in rounds, you answer, and after the last round it drafts a one-page work order. Spring service week for the bike workshop The AI asks · you answer Round 1 · the goal Who is the week for: regulars or new riders? What must be ready before the spring rush? 1. Regulars first. 2. Every rental bike serviced. Round 2 · the limits Who books the slots, and how? Which bikes are out of scope? 1. Front desk, by phone and walk-in. 2. E-bikes, they go to the partner shop. Round 3 · done when How will we know it’s done? “40 repair slots booked; exact deadline to confirm.” in rounds, not one by one Open details marked. Drafting the spec. Draft spec · Spring service week For Regulars first Must Every rental bike serviced Booked by Front desk, phone and walk-in Out E-bikes Done when 40 slots; exact deadline to confirm First page on a clean bench

Creating context for agents (3/3) Page 3 of 3 BRIEF The five moves from the freelancer Episode, and today's session shows three of the five: R, I and F. Freelancer · AI · Day 1 Callback: Onboard AI every time B Break it down Not today R Requirements first Today: context frames the work, but is not the same as a requirements document I Interview with AI Today: the grill, in rounds of questions E Evaluate each step Not today F Fresh chat Today: carry the spec into a new chat, not the long one

A thought experiment No speaker notes for this Slide.

What the customer really wanted Why the line gets out of balance DORA's 2025 report overview says AI's primary role is as an amplifier, magnifying an organization's existing strengths and weaknesses, and that the greatest returns come from a focus on the organizational system rather than the tools. It is an overview page; the report text was not read 1 . Sources (1) DORA, State of AI-assisted Software Development 2025 (overview page) ( opens in a new tab ) dora.dev

What happens with AI Measured: the load moves to review In Faros's observational sample of software teams with high AI adoption, developers completed 21% more tasks and merged 98% more pull requests; review time rose 91% and pull requests grew 154%. The report found no statistically significant company-level productivity improvement in that sample 1 . These are sample findings, not a universal or causal prediction. Sources (1) Faros AI, The AI Productivity Paradox Report 2025 (23 July 2025) ( opens in a new tab ) faros.ai Engineers say the same Google engineers report that the time saved in creating is re-spent on auditing and verifying, and DORA reads this as work moving from authors to reviewers 1 . Sources (1) DORA, Balancing AI tensions ( opens in a new tab ) dora.dev What is measured and what is inferred The report observes more review time and larger pull requests in its sample; it does not establish that unclear specifications caused those changes. The findings are observational, vendor-reported software-team data, not a universal or causal prediction 1 . Sources (1) Faros AI, The AI Productivity Paradox Report 2025 (23 July 2025) ( opens in a new tab ) faros.ai

Speed the whole line can carry Returns come from the system DORA's overview reports that the greatest returns from AI come from a strategic focus on the underlying organizational system, not the tools. This is an overview page, so treat it as a pointer 1 . Sources (1) DORA, State of AI-assisted Software Development 2025 (overview page) ( opens in a new tab ) dora.dev
Why precise and accurate requirements mattered before AI No speaker notes for this Slide.

Value was always translation The hard part is the concept Brooks argues the hard part of building software is deciding what to build, the conceptual construct, and not the labor of representing it in code; an error in the concept cripples the result and is hardest to rectify later 1 . Sources (1) Brooks, No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering ( opens in a new tab ) cgl.ucsf.edu How strong the evidence is this is one author's argument from experience, written in 1986 about human-built software. No source compares requirements and execution on the same projects, and that it holds when an AI builds is an inference 1 . Sources (1) Brooks, No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering ( opens in a new tab ) cgl.ucsf.edu

Defining and building Clients cannot state it up front Brooks holds that clients do not know what they want and cannot specify it completely and correctly before they have tried versions of the product, so refining requirements iteratively is what builders do most for them 1 . Sources (1) Brooks, No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering ( opens in a new tab ) cgl.ucsf.edu Practitioners name it too in a survey of 228 companies, incomplete or hidden requirements were the most cited requirements problem (48%), and avoidable rework is estimated at 40 to 50 percent of project effort, though the 100x late-fix rule and the CHAOS failure rates are disputed 1 . Sources (1) Why do unclear requirements lead to rework and failed projects? (earlier research file) ( opens in a new tab ) github.com

Precision and accuracy Missing requirements show up as wrong output in 55 historic aerospace software incidents, 85% produced wrong output instead of stopping, only 16% were errors of traditional programming, and 40% came from absent code, meaning missing requirements or unanticipated situations 1 . Sources (1) Prokop, Historical Aerospace Software Errors Categorized to Influence Fault Tolerance ( opens in a new tab ) ntrs.nasa.gov Limits the 40% mixes missing requirements with unanticipated situations, the categories were assigned in hindsight, and the author doubts that more requirements would have averted many of these errors 1 . A survey of specifications found that how much quality matters depends on the project 2 . Sources (2) Prokop, Historical Aerospace Software Errors Categorized to Influence Fault Tolerance ( opens in a new tab ) ntrs.nasa.gov Mund, Femmer, Méndez Fernández, Eckhardt, Does Quality of Requirements Specifications matter? Combined Results of Two Empirical Studies ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org
Context and requirements No speaker notes for this Slide.

What the AI actually sees The window has an attention budget Anthropic says recall decreases as the number of tokens in the window increases, so context has diminishing marginal returns and an attention budget 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

Context engineering and requirements: a useful analogy Google’s definition Three Google authors define context engineering as “the practice of providing AI agents with rich, structured information about your codebase, architecture, conventions, and intent”, and list six kinds of context: instructions, knowledge, memory, examples, tools and guardrails. It is a practitioner whitepaper, not a study: it frames the term and does not test the parallel to requirements 1 . Sources (1) Osmani, Saboo, Kartakis (Google), The New SDLC With Vibe Coding: From ad-hoc prompting to Agentic Engineering ( opens in a new tab ) kaggle.com The definition Anthropic defines context engineering as curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens during inference, guided by "the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens" that maximize the chance of the desired outcome 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Input quality tracks output quality in a randomized experiment with 30 novices, training in requirement-oriented prompting beat conventional prompt-engineering training (20% against 1% gains), and the authors report input-requirement quality correlates with output quality. It is a small trip-advisor chatbot study, not coding agents 1 . Sources (1) Ma, Peng, Yang, Shen, Koedinger, Wu, What Should We Engineer in Prompts? Training Humans in Requirement-Driven LLM Use ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org A proposal, not a finding researchers have proposed the parallel, but no source measured whether the disciplines are equivalent; treating them as the same discipline would go beyond the evidence 1 . Sources (1) Chen, Wang, Sun, Liu, Zhang, Liu, Promptware Engineering: Software Engineering for Prompt-Enabled Systems ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Where the parallel stops a requirements document gains from completeness while a context window is a finite budget that can lose from it, and context changes during a run instead of being signed off once 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

Static and dynamic context Dynamic means loaded at run time agents can keep lightweight identifiers such as file paths and links, then use tools to load selected data into context at run time instead of loading everything up front 1 . The available sources depend on the agent's setup; people can limit access and review retrieved material. Sources (1) Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

You run the bench A result from one GPT-4o test In one specific GPT-4o test, compliance was 98.7% with one requirement and 85.0% with 19 requirements at once 1 . This result is limited to that test; it does not show that more instructions always reduce compliance. Separately, a study of repository context files did not find a general benefit from restating discoverable information 2 . Sources (2) content-library research, Why do explicit written requirements reduce the variation in LLM output? ( opens in a new tab ) github.com Gloaguen, Mündler-Sasahara, Müller, Raychev, Vechev, Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents? (v3, 2026-09-29) ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

Context rot Length alone does part of the damage in the cited study's tested setup, output quality declined as the context window filled, even with perfect retrieval 1 . This does not show that every model and task behaves the same. Sources (1) content-library research, Why does a language model's output quality drop as its context window fills? ( opens in a new tab ) github.com The four names Drew Breunig named context poisoning, distraction, confusion and clash in June 2025: poisoning is an error that gets saved and reused, distraction a long history that steers the model, confusion superfluous material such as surplus tools, clash conflicting material in the window 1 . Sources (1) Drew Breunig, How Long Contexts Fail ( opens in a new tab ) dbreunig.com Credit and limit the IBM Technology video presents the same four. The taxonomy is a practitioner blog post and a failure can fit more than one mode 1 . Sources (1) IBM Technology, Context Engineering for AI Agents: 4 Failure Modes to Avoid ( opens in a new tab ) youtube.com Numbers for confusion and clash Breunig cites Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard results where larger tool sets hurt selection in the tested comparisons; one quantized Llama 3.1 8B result failed with 46 tools and succeeded with 19. A separate multi-turn study reported a 39% average score drop when instructions were split across turns; that is not the same as asking clarifying questions 1 . Sources (1) Drew Breunig, How Long Contexts Fail ( opens in a new tab ) dbreunig.com

Keeping the bench clean The video's framing IBM Technology presents validate, compact, curate and prune as one fix for each of four failure modes. This is a teaching framework, not an exhaustive or exclusive mapping; real problems can overlap and one fix can help with more than one mode 1 . Sources (1) IBM Technology, Context Engineering for AI Agents: 4 Failure Modes to Avoid ( opens in a new tab ) youtube.com Breunig lists other fixes his companion post names six: RAG, tool loadout, context quarantine, pruning, summarization and offloading. Picking fewer than 30 tools improved selection accuracy up to threefold 1 . Sources (1) Drew Breunig, How to Fix Your Context ( opens in a new tab ) dbreunig.com One fix per mode is a simplification failure modes and fixes can overlap: compaction may preserve a bad fact in a clean summary, so it does not necessarily repair poisoning. The connection between a fresh window and both compact and prune is an inference. Anthropic also warns that overly aggressive compaction can lose subtle but critical context 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com
Creating context for agents No speaker notes for this Slide.

Meta prompting Questions can draw out richer answers In a study on preference elicitation, users' answers to model questions were often more informative than prompts they wrote unaided, and users reported less effort 1 . This does not show that everyone always answers better, or that the finding applies to every task. Sources (1) Li et al., Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Prompts generated from requirements REprompt builds a multi-agent prompt optimizer from requirements-engineering principles; the abstract reports effective optimization without numbers, and it is an early preprint 1 . Sources (1) Shi, Sun, Chen, Wu, Chen, Jin, Liu, REprompt: Prompt Generation for Intelligent Software Development Guided by Requirements Engineering ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

Grill-me Where grill-me comes from grill-me is a skill Matt Pocock published in his open collection of agent skills, "Skills for Real Engineers" 1 . He presents the collection's end-to-end coding workflow in a video 2 . Sources (2) Matt Pocock, mattpocock/skills: Skills for Real Engineers (GitHub) ( opens in a new tab ) github.com mattpocock/skills: A complete AI Coding workflow, end-to-end (YouTube) ( opens in a new tab ) youtube.com Clarifying questions can help on unclear tasks on an underspecified variant of SWE-Bench Verified, agents that interacted with the user to fill missing information improved by up to 74% over non-interactive ones; that is a maximum, from simulated users, and models struggled to tell which tasks need a question 1 . Sources (1) Vijayvargiya et al., Ambig-SWE: Interactive Agents to Overcome Underspecificity in Software Engineering ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Rounds are inferred the research backs asking clarifying questions before the task; "in rounds" is an inference. Separately, scores fell 39% on average when an instruction arrived over several turns, which measures piecemeal instructions and not clarifying questions 1 . Sources (1) Laban et al., LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

BRIEF Why a fresh chat Anthropic describes compaction as summarizing the contents and starting a new context window with the summary, warns that overly aggressive compaction can lose subtle but critical context, and recommends sub-agents with clean windows that return a condensed summary 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

A thought experiment 0:00 – 0:35 Imagine your organization as a line This is a thought experiment, not a measured prediction: faster work does not guarantee the right result. Imagine your organization as a factory line, with documents moving from one work center to the next, a request here, a design there, a finished result at the end. You already know this picture. The old cartoon shows a customer asking for a tire swing and getting a tangle of ropes, because each station built its own version of what the customer asked for. 0:35 – 1:00 Where this is going Before we start, here is the route. First, imagine what might happen if AI sped up work at each station. Then we look at what you hand the AI, because it can shape the result. And last, you will see how an AI interview can help build that handover, so you do not have to write it alone.

What the customer really wanted 0:00 – 0:18 The Hook That is the point from a moment ago: a wrong swing can be built faster. This is an illustration, not a measured promise. Keep it in mind as we look at what can shape the result and what you can do about it. 0:18 – 0:36 Cartoon to balanced line Now picture the cartoon turning into a real factory line. Input comes in at a steady rate, stations keep pace, and the output is steady. If work flowed this smoothly in your organization, there might be less to solve here. 0:36 – 0:57 Reality Real work does not always flow like the cartoon. A change at one station can create a queue elsewhere, but the effect depends on the work. Trying to speed up every step does not guarantee better flow. Look at the line you work in and ask yourself: which station is yours?

What happens with AI 0:00 – 0:29 Every station faster Now imagine giving every station an AI assistant. In this thought experiment, some work gets faster, but a line can still bottleneck. Faros's 2025 report observed more tasks and pull requests, alongside more review time and larger pull requests, in its sample of software teams with high AI adoption. That does not prove unclear specifications caused the review load, or that every team will see the same pattern. 0:29 – 0:50 Moving bottleneck When one part of a process speeds up, another part can become the bottleneck. In our example, that is the review station. The work has not vanished; the queue illustrates one way a bottleneck might shift. Whether that happens, and why, depends on the work and the team.
